titleStmt.title: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness
titleStmt.author: David J. Chalmers

bibl.title: Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: critique
span.quote: I critique some recent work that uses reductive methods to address consciousness, and argue that these methods inevitably fail to come to grips with the hardest part of the problem.

span.label: conscious experience
span.quote: The really hard problem of consciousness is the problem of experience.

span.label: conceptual-analysis
span.term: conceptual-analysis
span.quote: Philosophical analysis is also useful in getting value for money out of the data we have.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE FIELD'S PROBLEMS ARE DIVIDED BY THE METHOD THAT ADDRESSES THEM, NOT BY SUBJECT MATTER: the easy problems are DEFINED as those directly susceptible to the standard methods of cognitive science - explanation in terms of computational or neural mechanisms - and the hard ones as those that seem to RESIST those methods. The dividing principle is tractability by an instrument
span.quote: The easy problems of consciousness are those that seem directly susceptible to the standard methods of cognitive science, whereby a phenomenon is explained in terms of computational or neural mechanisms. The hard problems are those that seem to resist those methods.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE CENTRAL TERM IS DECLARED AMBIGUOUS BEFORE ANYTHING IS CLAIMED ABOUT IT: consciousness is said to be an ambiguous term referring to MANY DIFFERENT PHENOMENA, each needing explanation and some easier than others - so the paper's first move is to deny that its subject is one thing
span.quote: There is not just one problem of consciousness. “Consciousness” is an ambiguous term, referring to many different phenomena. Each of these phenomena needs to be explained, but some are easier to explain than others.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ONE WORD IS SHOWN CARRYING SEVERAL OPERATIONAL SENSES AT ONCE, each attaching to a different test: a state is called conscious when it is VERBALLY REPORTABLE, or when it is INTERNALLY ACCESSIBLE; a system is conscious OF information when it can react on that basis, or attends to it, or integrates it into control of behaviour; an action is conscious when DELIBERATE; an organism is conscious when AWAKE
span.quote: For example, one sometimes says that a mental state is conscious when it is verbally reportable, or when it is internally accessible. Sometimes a system is said to be conscious of some information when it has the ability to react on the basis of that information, or, more strongly, when it attends to that information, or when it can integrate that information and exploit it in the sophisticated control of behavior. We sometimes say that an action is conscious precisely when it is deliberate. Often, we say that an organism is conscious as another way of saying that it is awake.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A VOCABULARY SPLIT IS PROPOSED AND THE COST OF NOT ADOPTING IT IS NAMED: reserve the word for the phenomena of experience and use the LESS LOADED term `awareness` for the straightforward ones - and the stated consequence of the present situation is that those who talk about consciousness are FREQUENTLY TALKING PAST EACH OTHER
span.quote: Another useful way to avoid confusion (used by e.g., Newell 1990; Chalmers 1996) is to reserve the term “consciousness” for the phenomena of experience, using the less loaded term “awareness” for the more straightforward phenomena described earlier. If such a convention were widely adopted, communication would be much easier; as things stand, those who talk about “consciousness” are frequently talking past each other.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A BAIT-AND-SWITCH IS ANATOMISED AS A RECURRING GENRE IN THE LITERATURE, not as a mistake by any one author: the theory delivered TURNS OUT TO BE a theory of one of the more straightforward phenomena - reportability, introspective access, OR WHATEVER - after which the author declares the problem tractable after all, leaving the reader FEELING LIKE THE VICTIM OF A BAIT-AND-SWITCH while the hard problem remains untouched
span.quote: Upon examination, this theory turns out to be a theory of one of the more straightforward phenomena—of reportability, of introspective access, or whatever. At the close, the author declares that consciousness has turned out to be tractable after all, but the reader is left feeling like the victim of a bait-and-switch. The hard problem remains untouched.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TEST IS GIVEN FOR WHETHER A TERM IS EXHAUSTED BY A FUNCTION, AND IT IS A TEST ON THE RESIDUAL QUESTION: someone who says the verbal-report function has been explained BUT NOT reportability is making a TRIVIAL CONCEPTUAL MISTAKE, because ALL IT COULD POSSIBLY TAKE to explain reportability is an explanation of how the relevant function is performed - and the same is said to go for the others
span.quote: To see that this sort of thing is a conceptual fact, note that someone who says “you have explained the performance of the verbal report function, but you have not explained reportability” is making a trivial conceptual mistake about reportability. All it could possibly take to explain reportability is an explanation of how the relevant function is performed; the same goes for the other phenomena in question.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE SAME TEST IS RUN ON THE CONTRAST CASES AND COMES OUT THE OTHER WAY: after every cognitive and behavioural function in the vicinity has been explained there MAY STILL REMAIN A FURTHER UNANSWERED QUESTION - why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience - and the paper states flatly that THERE IS NO ANALOGOUS FURTHER QUESTION in the explanation of genes, or of life, or of learning. One test, several terms, opposite verdicts
span.quote: note that even when we have explained the performance of all the cognitive and behavioral functions in the vicinity of experience—perceptual discrimination, categorization, internal access, verbal report—there may still remain a further unanswered question: Why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience? A simple explanation of the functions leaves this question open. There is no analogous further question in the explanation of genes, or of life, or of learning.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE METHODS ARE SAID TO BE FITTED TO A CLASS OF PROBLEM BY DESIGN, WHICH IS WHY A RESIDUE REMAINS: the usual methods were developed PRECISELY to explain the performance of cognitive functions and do a good job of it - and as they stand they are ONLY equipped for that, so on the remaining problem the standard approach HAS NOTHING TO SAY. The gap is attributed to the instrument's design, not to insufficient effort
span.quote: These methods have been developed precisely to explain the performance of cognitive functions, and they do a good job of it. But as these methods stand, they are only equipped to explain the performance of functions. When it comes to the hard problem, the standard approach has nothing to say.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A THEORY IS SHOWN TO BE UNABLE TO EXPLAIN THE VERY LINK IT RELIES ON: the account GAINS ITS PURCHASE by assuming a connection between binding and experience, AND SO CAN DO NOTHING TO EXPLAIN THAT LINK - with the converse stated as the diagnostic, that if the link were understood the neurophysiological detail would be ICING ON THE CAKE
span.quote: If we do not know why binding and storage should give rise to experience, telling a story about the oscillations cannot help us. Conversely, if we knew why binding and storage gave rise to experience, the neurophysiological details would be just the icing on the cake. Crick and Koch’s theory gains its purchase by assuming a connection between binding and experience, and so can do nothing to explain that link.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A RESEARCHER'S OWN DEFINITION OF HIS TERM, IN HIS OWN WORDS: he sets the really difficult aspects aside as possibly having NO SCIENTIFIC SOLUTION, proposes to focus on things that are EASIER TO STUDY, describes someone noticing a cappuccino and reaching for it - and closes THAT'S WHAT I CALL AWARENESS. The term is given its scope by an example of responding in a meaningful manner
span.quote: Well, let’s first forget about the really difficult aspects, like subjective feelings, for they may not have a scientific solution. The subjective state of play, of pain, of pleasure, of seeing blue, of smelling a rose—there seems to be a huge jump between the materialistic level, of explaining molecules and neurons, and the subjective level. Let’s focus on things that are easier to study—like visual awareness. You’re now talking to me, but you’re not looking at me, you’re looking at the cappuccino, and so you are aware of it. You can say, “It’s a cup and there’s some liquid in it.” If I give it to you, you’ll move your arm and you’ll take it—you’ll respond in a meaningful manner. That’s what I call awareness.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ELIMINATION BY REDEFINITION IS NAMED AS A MOVE: some deny the phenomenon outright, and OTHERS ACHIEVE THE SAME EFFECT by allowing that experience exists ONLY IF the word is equated with something like the capacity to discriminate and report. The denial is performed by the definition rather than by an argument
span.quote: Some explicitly deny the phenomenon, holding for example that what is not externally verifiable cannot be real. Others achieve the same effect by allowing that experience exists, but only if we equate “experience” with something like the capacity to discriminate and report.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CRITERION IS GIVEN FOR WHEN A TERM MAY LEGITIMATELY BE RETIRED, AND IT TURNS ON THE TERM'S ROLE RATHER THAN ITS TRUTH: the vital spirit was put forward AS AN EXPLANATORY POSIT, to explain certain functions, AND COULD THEREFORE BE DISCARDED once those functions were explained without it - whereas an EXPLANANDUM IN ITS OWN RIGHT is not a candidate for that kind of elimination
span.quote: The vital spirit was put forward as an explanatory posit, in order to explain the relevant functions, and could therefore be discarded when those functions were explained without it. Experience is not an explanatory posit but an explanandum in its own right, and so is not a candidate for this sort of elimination.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE OBVIOUS PRECEDENT IS RAISED AND THE DISANALOGY IS LOCATED PRECISELY IN WHAT WAS EVER IN DOUBT: vitalist scepticism was doubt about whether physical mechanisms COULD PERFORM THE FUNCTIONS - while the conceptual claim that explanation of functions IS WHAT IS NEEDED was IMPLICITLY ACCEPTED by both sides. The historical parallel is disarmed by separating the empirical bet from the conceptual premise it never touched
span.quote: What drove vitalist skepticism was doubt about whether physical mechanisms could perform the many remarkable functions associated with life, such as complex adaptive behavior and reproduction. The conceptual claim that explanation of functions is what is needed was implicitly accepted

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A FALLACY ABOUT HOW TWO TERMS COME TO BE LINKED IS NAMED AND GIVEN A LAW: the attractiveness of quantum theories of consciousness is attributed to a LAW OF MINIMIZATION OF MYSTERY - consciousness is mysterious and quantum mechanics is mysterious, SO MAYBE THE TWO MYSTERIES HAVE A COMMON SOURCE. The proposed connection is between the two terms' obscurity, not between their contents
span.quote: The attractiveness of quantum theories of consciousness may stem from a Law of Minimization of Mystery: consciousness is mysterious and quantum mechanics is mysterious, so maybe the two mysteries have a common source.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CLASS OF THEORY IS SHOWN TO RUN THE EXPLANATION BACKWARDS: these theories ASSUME THE EXISTENCE of consciousness and USE IT IN THE EXPLANATION of quantum processes. The term appears in the explanans where it was wanted in the explanandum
span.quote: Rather, these theories assume the existence of consciousness, and use it in the explanation of quantum processes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TEMPTING INDUCTION FROM THE HISTORY OF SCIENCE IS NAMED AND BLOCKED BY SORTING ITS CASES: it is tempting to note that puzzling phenomena have always eventually yielded to physical explanation - but EACH of those was a problem about the observable behaviour of physical objects, coming down to structures and functions, and therefore always the KIND OF THING a physical account might explain. The induction fails because its instances share a property the new case lacks
span.quote: It is tempting to note that all sorts of puzzling phenomena have eventually turned out to be explainable in physical terms. But each of these were problems about the observable behavior of physical objects, coming down to problems in the explanation of structures and functions. Because of this, these phenomena have always been the kind of thing that a physical account might explain, even if at some points there have been good reasons to suspect that no such explanation would be forthcoming. The tempting induction from these cases fails in the case of consciousness

span.label: The proposed theory is offered as speculative and only a candidate.
span.note: what this limits: the positive proposal only: THE THEORY I HAVE PRESENTED IS SPECULATIVE, BUT IT IS A CANDIDATE THEORY
span.quote: The theory I have presented is speculative, but it is a candidate theory.

span.label: The central basic principle (double-aspect theory of information) is admitted to be highly speculative and to leave key questions open.
span.note: what this limits: the double-aspect principle specifically: IT IS EXTREMELY SPECULATIVE AND IS ALSO UNDERDETERMINED, LEAVING A NUMBER OF KEY QUESTIONS UNANSWERED
span.quote: Of course, the double-aspect principle is extremely speculative and is also underdetermined, leaving a number of key questions unanswered.

span.label: There is very little objective data on which to build a theory of consciousness, because experience is not directly observable.
span.note: what this limits: the evidence base for any theory of consciousness: THE PAUCITY OF OBJECTIVE DATA - experience is not directly observable
span.quote: There is an obvious problem that plagues the development of a theory of consciousness, and that is the paucity of objective data.

span.label: Theories of this kind cannot be settled by conclusive intersubjective experimental test and so keep a speculative element.
span.note: what this limits: the epistemic status of the whole class of theories, permanently: SUCH THEORIES WILL ALWAYS RETAIN AN ELEMENT OF SPECULATION ... BECAUSE OF THE IMPOSSIBILITY OF CONCLUSIVE INTERSUBJECTIVE EXPERIMENTAL TESTS
span.quote: Such theories will always retain an element of speculation that is not present in other scientific theories, because of the impossibility of conclusive intersubjective experimental tests.

span.label: The central term is stated to be ambiguous, and the paper says the ambiguity leads researchers to talk past one another.
span.note: what this limits: any claim about consciousness stated without saying which phenomenon is meant: the paper states people using the term are frequently talking past each other
span.quote: If such a convention were widely adopted, communication would be much easier; as things stand, those who talk about “consciousness” are frequently talking past each other.

span.label: The paper states the ambiguity of its central term is exploited by writers in both philosophy and science.
span.note: what this limits: a consciousness claim taken at face value: the paper states the term's ambiguity is often exploited by philosophers and scientists alike
span.quote: The ambiguity of the term “consciousness” is often exploited by both philosophers and scientists writing on the subject.

span.label: using the explanatory framework of cognitive science and neuroscience (computational and neural mechanisms) to demarcate the tractable easy problems of consciousness from the hard problem
span.quote: The easy problems of consciousness are those that seem directly susceptible to the standard methods of cognitive science

span.label: hard problem - the problem of experience: the subjective aspect that remains once the information-processing is accounted for
span.quote: The really hard problem of consciousness is the problem of experience. When we think and perceive, there is a whir of information-processing, but there is also a subjective aspect. As Nagel (1974) has put it, there is something it is like to be a conscious organism.

span.label: contradicts → reductive methods for explaining consciousness
span.note: differs in: which part of the problem is addressed: THESE METHODS INEVITABLY FAIL TO COME TO GRIPS WITH THE HARDEST PART OF THE PROBLEM
span.quote: these methods inevitably fail to come to grips with the hardest part of the problem

span.label: builds-on → Nagel (1974), 'What is it like to be a bat?'

span.label: builds-on → Levine (1983), the explanatory gap
span.quote: There is an explanatory gap (a term due to Levine 1983) between the functions and experience, and we need an explanatory bridge to cross it.

span.label: builds-on → Shannon (1948), information theory
span.quote: I understand information in more or less the sense of Shannon (1948).

span.label: contradicts → Crick and Koch (1990) neurobiological theory of consciousness (40-Hz binding oscillations)
span.note: differs in: what is assumed against what is explained: CRICK AND KOCH'S THEORY GAINS ITS PURCHASE BY ASSUMING A CONNECTION BETWEEN BINDING AND EXPERIENCE, AND SO CAN DO NOTHING TO EXPLAIN THAT LINK
span.quote: Crick and Koch’s theory gains its purchase by assuming a connection between binding and experience, and so can do nothing to explain that link.

span.label: contradicts → Bernard Baars, global workspace theory (A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness)
span.note: differs in: awareness against experience: THE THEORY SHOWS PROMISE AS A THEORY OF AWARENESS, THE FUNCTIONAL CORRELATE OF CONSCIOUS EXPERIENCE, BUT AN EXPLANATION OF EXPERIENCE ITSELF IS NOT ON OFFER
span.quote: The theory shows promise as a theory of awareness, the functional correlate of conscious experience, but an explanation of experience itself is not on offer.

span.label: contradicts → Searle (1980), biological naturalism about consciousness
span.note: differs in: whether the substrate matters: CONSCIOUSNESS IS TIED TO A SPECIFIC BIOLOGY, SO THAT A SILICON ISOMORPH OF A HUMAN NEED NOT BE CONSCIOUS - against organisation alone
span.quote: Some (e.g., Searle 1980) have thought that consciousness is tied to a specific biology, so that a silicon isomorph of a human need not be conscious.
